extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy (ethicists); legislators and moralists
extracted.subtask_description: Close analysis of voluntariness, moral choice (prohairesis), deliberation, formation of moral character, and the nature of Courage in Aristotelian virtue ethics, with criteria for ascribing praise, blame, allowance, and responsibility. Includes distinctions (voluntary vs involuntary vs not‑voluntary), scope of deliberation, and species/errors of Courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary vs Involuntary Actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary action: that whose origination is in the agent, the agent being aware of the particular details in which the action consists. Involuntary action: that which is done either on compulsion or by reason of ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish at the time of doing: voluntary when origination rests with the agent and he is aware of particulars; involuntary when caused by external compulsion or ignorance. Moral appraisal (praise/blame/allowance) hinges on this distinction: praise/blame for voluntary acts; allowance/compassion for truly involuntary ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory Actions (Action under Compulsion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An action is properly compulsory when its origination is external to the agent, and the party compelled contributes nothing to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: being carried by wind, being forced by men who have power over you. Mixed cases (e.g., ordered by a despot threatening parents) raise questions: if the agent's limbs originate motion within himself, it is more like voluntary. Persons acting under compulsion commonly act with pain; those acting from honour or pleasure act with pleasure. Legislators and judges should take account of compulsion when assigning honours or punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance‑based Involuntariness
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions caused by ignorance are not automatically involuntary; to be truly involuntary the ignorance must concern particulars of the action (who acts, what is done, in respect to what, with what instrument, with what result) and the action must be attended by pain and remorse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish ignorance of principle (blameworthy) from ignorance of particulars (excusing). Examples: speaking of the Mysteries without knowing it unlawful; discharging a device to 'display' it; mistaking a son for an enemy; intending to strike to save but killing. The more important the ignorant particulars (those in which the action consists and its result), the stronger the excuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not‑Voluntary (Ignorance without Regret)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an action is done by reason of ignorance but the agent feels no annoyance or regret afterwards, the action is 'not‑voluntary' rather than 'involuntary'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a distinct category: both involve ignorance, but involuntary actions are followed by pain/remorse while not‑voluntary lack that remorse. The distinction matters for moral terminology and assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed Cases / Actions under Necessity or Duress
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done from fear of greater evils or by necessity (e.g., throwing goods overboard in a storm) are of a mixed kind but most like voluntary actions because they are choice‑worthy at the time and the agent originates the motion of his limbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate these at the time of action: they may be praised if endured for great and honourable equivalents, blamed if endured for base or trifling reasons, or treated with allowance if they exceed human powers. The origin of the action in the agent (even under pressure) often makes them more like voluntary acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Choice (Prohairesis) — definition and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Choice is a voluntary grasping after something in our own power consequent upon deliberation; its object is the means to ends rather than the end itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral Choice is distinct from mere voluntary action because it presupposes prior deliberation; it is the faculty by which character expresses itself in chosen means. It is the decisive test of moral character and is exercised by those capable of deliberation (not animals or young children).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and Object of Deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation concerns matters that are within our own instrumentality and are means to ends; it does not deliberate about ends themselves, eternal or necessary truths, wholly fortuitous matters, or highly exact sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberation applies to practical matters where there is some indefiniteness and a choice of means. One stops deliberating once the origination rests with oneself. For great matters one may consult others. Do not deliberate about trivial sensory details or things impossible to affect by one’s own agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from Wish, Opinion, Anger, and Lust
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Choice is not identical with Wish, Opinion, Anger, or Lust: Wish concerns ends (possibly impossible), Opinion concerns truth/falsehood, and Anger/Lust are passions often shared with animals and opposed to deliberative choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinctions when attributing responsibility: wishes may be about what one cannot effect; opinions are not divided into good/bad as choices are; anger and lust frequently lead away from moral choice. Moral choice selects means one believes oneself capable of effecting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of Virtues through Habituation
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues are mean states and habits formed by repeated voluntary actions; while we may not perceive the incremental formation, the origination of the habits is in our power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral character is produced by practicing actions; persistence in certain acts builds corresponding habits. Thus becoming virtuous is a result of voluntary repeated acts even if the habit later constrains action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for Self‑caused Ignorance and Vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance that is self‑caused (e.g., through drunkenness, neglect of what one ought to know) is blameworthy; producing vices by voluntary acts makes one voluntarily vicious and subject to punishment or censure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drunkenness is culpable because one could have avoided getting drunk; ignorance of easily known laws attracts punishment. The law and moral judgment punish or withhold honor when ignorance is judged self‑caused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Evaluation: Praise, Blame, and Allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise and blame properly attach to voluntary actions; allowance/compassion is proper for involuntary ones; some acts may attract praise if endured for honourable ends, blame if endured for trivial or base motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess actions by whether they were voluntary, the motive (honour vs triviality), and the agent’s state (remorse or not). Legislators and communities use these distinctions in allocating honors and punishments to encourage virtue and restrain vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage as the Mean with Respect to Fear and Confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage is a mean state between excess and deficiency with reference to fear and boldness; its proper object‑matter is fear of things that are honourable to face (not all things feared), especially honourable death in war when death would be noble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Brave person resists or acts as right reason directs, in respect of right objects, from right motive (honour), in the right manner, and at the right time. Courage is exhibited where action admits of helping oneself and where death or danger can be honourable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors regarding Courage: Rashness, Cowardice, and Madness
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive confidence (rashness) and excessive fear (cowardice) are the corresponding vices to Courage; an utter absence of fear would be madness. All three relate to the same object‑matter but stand differently in relation to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rashness: precipitate, boastful, imitates bravery but fails in true danger. Cowardice: fears wrong objects or in wrong ways/times; faint‑hearted. Evaluate by motive, steadiness in action, and whether the agent stands firm as right reason directs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species/Variants of Courage (citizenship, compulsion, skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different dispositions bear the name 'Courage' by analogy: civic courage (motivated by shame and honour), courage produced by compulsion from commanders (lower form), and courage from experience/skill (soldiers trained by habituation/knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True Courage most properly arises from a sense of honour (not mere compulsion). Skill and habituation can give the appearance of courage, but such troops may be cowardly when danger exceeds their means. Distinguish the motive (honour vs compulsion vs habituation) when judging the quality of courage.
